implementation_notes: The filter class collapses into `java.util.function.Predicate`: `stream.filter(p)` keeps the matching elements and throws the rest away, and `Predicate.and/or/negate` compose criteria without new types; `Collection.removeIf(Predicate.not(p))` is the in-place form for buffered messages. A named MessageFilter class is still justified when the criterion comes from configuration or must be an injectable, testable component with its own state (counters, tenant rules).
pitfalls: Stream.filter does not mutate the source: without a terminal operation nothing happens at all - the classic 'my filter does nothing' bug.
A stream can be consumed once; reusing a filtered result means collecting it or calling `.stream()` again on the collection.
A predicate that throws (parsing a header, map lookup on a missing key) aborts the whole pipeline mid-stream - validate inside the predicate and decide explicitly.

variants.name: Declarative filter in the messaging layer (Camel / JMS selector)
variants.idiom_name: Apache Camel Filter EIP / JMS message selector
variants.implementation_notes: In integration code the criterion is configuration rather than a lambda: Camel's Filter EIP wraps route steps in a predicate - `.filter(simple("${header.foo} == 'bar'"))` - and its documentation states that messages whose predicate returns false are filtered out and not routed further, while JMS consumers pass a selector string to `createConsumer(destination, messageSelector)`. Filtering therefore happens in the route or broker before your handler runs, and Camel's `statusPropertyName` option records whether an exchange matched, which is how the decision stays observable. Choose it when interest changes per environment or tenant; keep the in-code Predicate when the criterion needs typed access to a deserialised payload, because selectors see headers and properties only.
pitfalls: Camel's filter EIP only guards its own children: without a `stop()` step the message continues down the route after the block, so a 'filtered' message can still be seen downstream (the Camel docs call this out explicitly).
Message selectors are evaluated by the broker against headers and properties only; a criterion that needs the body forces consumer-side filtering and full deserialisation.
Selector strings are neither compiled nor type-checked against the schema: a typo in a property name starves the consumer silently, so keep a contract test for the rule.
